newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Great Lakes conflict sparks exodus from Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Great Lakes conflict sparks exodus from Zaire.

text.p: Ethnic warfare engulfing eastern Zaire has sparked a new refugee crisis in Central Africa's Great Lakes region haunted by Hutu-Tutsi bloodshed.
Aid workers said half a million Hutus fleeing attacks on their refugee camps in Zaire were now streaming back towards Rwanda, the homeland they left in 1994 to escape massacres and civil war.
"Right now over 100,000 people have already arrived in Mugunga camp outside Goma," U.N. official Panos Moumtzis told Cable News Network from Goma on Sunday night.
Earlier he said: "There is a stream of people about 25 km (15 miles) long...I saw pregnant women, handicapped people, little children."

Refugees emptied their camps after a attack on Kibumba at the northwestern corner of Lake Kivu in which one Zairean guard and four refugees were killed, according to aid workers. A similar attack on Katale camp wounded three soldiers.
Many Zairean civilians were also on the run to try to escape spreading fighting between the Zaire army and ethnic Tutsi rebels.
For the Hutus, a return to Rwanda would be a gamble. Hutu refugees are afraid of reprisals for the genocide of Rwandan Tutsis in 1994 by Hutus.
Amid the panic and confusion, the United Nations appealed for states in the region to open up humanitarian corridors.

"A catastrophe greater than the one we knew in 1994 is what worries me most," U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees Sadako Ogata said in a statement in Geneva. "I appeal to the combatants: please spare the refugees and local populations."

Western nations advised their citizens to leave Zaire. The appeals came most notably from the three countries with the greatest clout in the tormented region -- the United States, France and Belgium, the former regional colonial power.

A Foreign Ministry spokesman in Brusssels said the Belgian embassy in Kinshasa had individually contacted the 230 Belgians still remaining in Zaire's war-torn provinces of north and south Kivu. Most are missionaries.
International aid agencies evacuated most of their staff from Bukavu, the South Kivu provincial capital, which was under threat of attack by the Banyamulenge Tutsi rebels.

The Banyamulenge rebels, from a 300,000-strong community that migrated from what is now Rwanda to Zaire 200 years ago, have already taken a string of towns in districts around Bukavu. They resisting orders to leave Zaire.
The armies of both Rwanda and Burundi, Zaire's small neighbours to the east, are dominated by the Tutsi minorities and diplomats fear they are being drawn into the conflict.
Diplomats said the Hutu refugees, pushed out of camps in Zaire, could launch attacks in northwest Burundi while attempting to reach Hutu refugee camps in Tanzania.
A central objective for both Burundi and Rwanda is the closure of the Hutu refugee camps located right on their borders and used as bases for Hutu rebel infiltrators.
Zaire says Rwanda is sending troops to support Tutsi rebels, a charge Rwanda denies.

"We have no problem with the Tutsis but we do have a problem with the Rwandan government which is trying to push 85 percent of its population (Hutus) on to Zairean soil," former Zairean prime minister Faustin Birindwa told Reuters in Bukavu.
Birindwa, who is from the Kivu area, said the rebels were attacking refugee camps to disperse the refugees and prevent them from reassembling and causing a security threat to Rwanda and Burundi.
